[13. Lakṣyayoga]
[XIII. Lakṣyayoga] \phantomsection Now, LakṣyayogaLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga (``Yoga of foci''),The original reading of the yoga is likely lakṣyayogaLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga since it is attested across both the \beta manuscript witnesses!\beta group and \gamma groupsmanuscript witnesses!\gamma group. This reading is supported by the usage in the ssplonavlaSiddhasiddhantapaddhati@Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati 2.26–32 and yogacandrikaYogacandrika@Yogacandrikā (Ed. p. 2). However, ramatosana (Ed. pp. 833–834) and yogakarnikaYogakarnika@Yogakarṇikā (Ed. pp. 23–24) as well as sarvangayogaSarvangayoga@Sarvāṅgayoga (Ed. pp. 104–105) use the term lakṣayoga, indicating that both designations were common. See p. for a detailed discussion of Lakṣyayoga.which is easily accomplished,The emphasis on the ease of Lakṣ(y)ayoga is not just shared with the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya but also with Sundardās'sSundardas@Sundardās sarvangayoga 3.25a: lakṣayoga hai sugam upāī |is explained. There are five subdivisions of this Lakṣyayoga: 1. The upper focus (ūrdhvalakṣya)Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!urdhvalaksya@ūrdhvalakṣya, 2. The lower focus (adholakṣya)Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!adholaksya@adholakṣya, 3. The outer focus (bāhyalakṣya)Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!bahyalaksya@bāhyalakṣya, 4. The middle focus (madhyalakṣya)Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!madhyalaksya@madhyalakṣya, 5. The inner focus (antaralakṣya)Laksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!antaralaksya@antaralakṣya.In most other texts it is called antarlakṣya, but the TattvayogabinduTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu reads antaralakṣya throughout its manuscript tradition. This is confirmed by the HaṭhasaṅketacandrikāHathasamketacandrika@Haṭhasaṅketacandrikā (cf. sources).The practices of Lakṣ(y)ayoga in Sundardās's sarvangayoga 3.35–36 (Ed. pp. 104–105) are essentially identical, except presented in a different order and subsumed under the category of HaṭhayogaHathayoga@Haṭhayoga. The ssplonavla, one of Rāmacandra'sRamacandra@Rāmacandra central sources, particularly for the second half of his text, describes three almost identical lakṣyas in 2.26–31: antarlakṣya, bahirlakṣya and madhyamaṃ lakṣyaṃ.NārāyaṇatīrthaNarayanatirtha@Nārāyaṇatīrtha, in his yogacandrika, does not mention any of the five categories within his descriptions of Lakṣyayoga. Here, Lakṣyayoga is connected to YogasūtraYogasutra@Yogasūtra 1.35. Lakṣyayoga directs the mind onto a specific focus, like the tip of the nose, etc., to stop the mind's activity, cf. yogacandrika, Ed. p. 54.\flushpage

[14. The upper focus]
[XIV. The upper focus] \phantomsection At first, the upper focusLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!urdhvalaksya@ūrdhvalakṣya is explained. The gaze is on the centre of the sky.This could be the zenith; see petersburger3.And then, having directed the mind upwards, it is fixed [there]. As a result of stabilising this focus, unity of the gaze with the splendour of the highest lord arises. And then, some object that has not been seen before arises in the centre of the sky. That [object] arises in the range of sight of the practitioner. This alone is the upper focus.SundardāsSundardas@Sundardās presents a comparable understanding of ūrdhvalakṣ(y)a, namely the practice of fixing the gaze on the sky, in his sarvangayogaSarvangayoga@Sarvāṅgayoga 3.27: ūrddha lakṣa karai ihīṃ bhāṃtī | duṣṭyākāśa rahai dina rātī | bibidha prakāra hoi ujiyārā | gopi padāratha dīsahiṃ sārā ||A similar practice is presented in bäumer2013 84: ākāśaṃ vimalam paśyan kṛtvā dṛṣṭiṃ nirantarām | stabdhātmā tatkṣaṇād devi bhairavaṃ vapur āpnuyāt || Although the term lakṣya is not used, the central elements of the practice are found here: the gaze is constantly fixed on the sky, establishing a connection with the divine. See also mallinson2007 5.30–31.\flushpage

[15. The lower focus] 1mm
[XV. The lower focus] \phantomsection Now, the lower focusLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga!adholaksya@adholakṣya. One should stabilize the gaze up to twelve finger breadths above the nose. Alternatively, one should stabilize the gaze onto the tip of the nose. The gaze becomes still due to the stabilising of the two foci. The breath becomes stable. Lifespan increases.In Sundardās'sSundardas@Sundardās sarvangayogaSarvangayoga@Sarvāṅgayoga 2.26 (Ed. p. 104), one finds the following verse with a similar concept. He shares the technique of fixing the gaze onto the nose and the notion of the breath becoming stabilised: prathamahīṃ adho lakṣa kauṃ jānaiṃ | nāśā agra dṛṣṭi sthira ānaiṃ | yātoṃ mana pavanā thira hoī | adho lakṣa jo sādhai koī ||In his hathasamketacandrikachennaiHathasamketacandrika@Haṭhasaṅketacandrikā, SundaradevaSundaradeva@Sundaradeva adds further techniques to the category of adholakṣya at this point of the text. For the reconstructed passage (based on ORI B220, GOML R3239, and MMPP 2244) and its translation, see p.~.This pair is also taught as an external focus.This statement associates the two practices of adholakṣya with bāhyalakṣya, which is described later in the text. Indeed, these later descriptions instruct the practitioner to focus on one of the five elements at various distances in front of the nose or above the head (cf. p. ).[Then] the focus of emptiness, which is like space, should be executed internally and externally.The description undoubtedly derives from the YogasvarodayaYogasvarodaya@Yogasvarodaya as quoted in the ramatosana (Ed. p. 834), where it is declared a practice of antaralakṣ(y)a. RāmacandraRamacandra@Rāmacandra extracts this passage from his source text and locates this practice within the adholakṣya category.The fear of death does not arise due to meditation on the void in all states while eating, moving, waking [and] at the time of rest.The translation of sthitikāle as ``time of rest'' is confirmed by the four states mentioned in the YSv (cf. sources). The formulation sthitikāle is Rāmacandra's rendering of suṣupteṣu.The concept of five lakṣ(y)as appears only in the lost Yogasvarodaya and from there made its way into ramatosana, yogakarnikaYogakarnika@Yogakarṇikā and TattvayogabinduTattvayogabindu@Tattvayogabindu. Other texts that include it are sarvangayoga, hathasamketacandrikamysore and yogacandrikaYogacandrika@Yogacandrikā. In those texts, it is treated as a distinct type of yoga: Lakṣ(y)yogaLaksyayoga@Lakṣyayoga. If one encounters the concept of three lakṣ(y)a as found in netratantraNetratantra@Netratantra (cf. 7.1), shivayogapradipikaSivayogapradipika@Śivayogapradīpikā (cf. 4.36–50), mandalabrah (cf. 2.6–2.14) or advaya (Ed. pp. 3–5) etc. it is never presented as a distinct type of yoga.
